newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish govt trails 12 points in pre-election poll.
newsitem.headline: Irish govt trails 12 points in pre-election poll.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton's coalition is trailing opposition parties by 12 points in the runup to June 6 elections, according to an opinion poll published in newspapers on Thursday.
The poll, the first since Bruton announced the election date on May 15, showed that his three-party "Rainbow Coalition" has failed to narrow the gap since the last survey in April.
The last survey showed Bruton's alliance trailing the opposition by 11 points before a poll being contested on the issues of taxation, crime and unemployment.
Thursday's poll showed that the grouping of Bruton's Fine Gael, Labour Party and Democratic Left would poll 38 per cent of support in the election.
But the rival centre-right opposition allies of Fianna Fail, led by Bertie Ahern, and Mary Harney's Progressive Democrats, would win 50 per cent of the vote, the survey said.
The survey showed individual party support as follows: Fine Gael, 26 per cent, unchanged; Labour 10 per cent, down two points; Democratic Left two per cent, no change.

Fianna Fail would draw an unchanged 43 per cent and the Progressive Democrats seven per cent, one point down on the previous survey, with the remainder of votes going to the Green party or Independents.
But the survey brought some good news for Bruton's government, which came to power at the end of 1994 after the previous Fianna Fail-led government of former Prime Minister Albert Reynolds collapsed.
Asked which coalition they would prefer, an unchanged 44 per cent said they would prefer the opposiiton alliance of Fianna Fail and Progressive Democrats.

But 38 per cent said they would favour the current left-right coalition, an increase of six points over the previous survey. Eight per cent of people wold prefer neither coalition and 10 per cent were undecided.

The main loser in the latest survey of 1,000 voters carried out on May 19 and 20 by the MRBI agency for the Irish Times appeared to be the Labour party of Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Dick Spring.
Spring's party pulled out its support for the Reynolds government in a row over legal appointments and switched its backing to Bruton and his junior Democratic Left ally.
Ireland uses proportional representation for its elections. No Irish government has been returned to power for a second term at an election since 1969.
Campaigning has been dominated by rival plans for tax cuts. Fianna Fail has promised to bring down the top 48 per cent tax rate by five points over a five-year period.
But the government has promised to carry out its own reforms by widening tax bands and raising allowances to ease the taxation burden.
